title: Optimal training-conditional regret for online conformal prediction
research_question: How can online conformal prediction maintain strong training-conditional coverage guarantees under unknown abrupt or smooth distribution drift, including when prediction models themselves are updated online?
methodology: The paper defines training-conditional cumulative regret as the accumulated absolute deviation of conditional prediction-set coverage from its target and studies independent observations under either change-point or smoothly drifting distributions. For independently pretrained nonconformity scores it proposes DriftOCP, which uses repeated drift detection and adaptive calibration-window resets, and proves upper bounds together with matching minimax lower bounds. For scores trained from streaming data it develops DriftOCP-full, replacing permutation-symmetry assumptions with Lipschitz and algorithmic-stability conditions and deriving non-asymptotic guarantees. Synthetic regression experiments compare the drift-aware methods with adaptive conformal inference variants under stationary, abrupt, and smoothly changing environments.

key_findings.finding: For pretrained scores, DriftOCP attains regret of order approximately sqrt((Ncp+1)T) under change points and sqrt(T) plus KS_T^(1/3)T^(2/3) under smooth score-distribution drift, up to logarithmic factors.

The corresponding minimax lower bounds match the pretrained-score upper-bound dependence on the horizon and drift measures up to logarithmic factors, establishing minimax optimality within the stated admissible algorithm class.

For online-trained scores under the stated Lipschitz and stability assumptions, DriftOCP-full attains regret of order approximately sqrt((Ncp+L+1)T) for change points and sqrt((L+1)T) plus TV_T^(1/3)T^(2/3) for smooth drift.
The full-conformal analysis also yields a batch training-conditional coverage concentration result for stable data-dependent predictors without requiring permutation-invariant model fitting.

In the pretrained-score simulations, DriftOCP remained comparatively stable in stationary segments while adapting rapidly after shifts, whereas ACI exhibited a stepsize trade-off between stable calibration and rapid reaction to drift.

key_findings.finding: The online-model experiments illustrate that adapting the fitted predictive model as well as recalibrating prediction sets can improve interval efficiency while keeping empirical coverage near its target under covariate shift.
key_findings.section: 5.2 Experiments: Online Conformal Prediction with Adaptively Trained Scores

limitations: The theoretical guarantees rely on independence across observations and do not cover temporally dependent non-stationary processes such as general Markov or time-series environments.

The online-trained-score guarantees require stability of the fitting algorithm and Lipschitz regularity; these conditions can fail or be difficult to establish for high-dimensional, nonparametric, or deep models.
The lower-bound result for the full-conformal setting restricts prediction procedures to sets representable as a union of at most K intervals.
The numerical evaluation is synthetic rather than an evaluation on naturally occurring non-stationary data streams.

The pretrained-score experimental protocol states that experiments were repeated 40 times, while the Figure 3 caption states that its curves were averaged over 20 runs, leaving an ambiguity in the reported replication count.
raw_claims: The paper evaluates online conformal prediction using training-conditional cumulative coverage regret rather than only long-run marginal coverage frequency.
The non-stationarity model covers both abrupt change points and gradually evolving distributions.
DriftOCP detects distribution changes and adapts which recent observations are used for conformal calibration.
For pretrained scores, the upper regret bounds match derived minimax lower bounds up to logarithmic factors.
DriftOCP-full is designed for settings in which the prediction model and resulting nonconformity score change with incoming observations.
The full-conformal analysis substitutes stability conditions for the permutation symmetry often used in conformal theory.
The smooth-drift bound for pretrained scores depends on drift in score distributions measured through a Kolmogorov-Smirnov quantity.
The corresponding adaptive-model smooth-drift bound uses total variation between data distributions.
The simulation horizon in the first experiment is 10,000 time steps with target miscoverage 0.1.
Extending the training-conditional theory to dependent non-stationary sequences is left as future work.
